Your left knee, part 2: cycling, the gym, the cartilage crack and the marathon

This page builds on the first one (knee.html): same MRI, same model, three new questions. In short, the MRI shows a kneecap that sits and rides outward in a shallow-at-the-top groove (8 mm shift, TT-TG 17 mm), mildly irritated quadriceps and patellar tendons, and a tiny crack in the cartilage of the kneecap's outer facet with some irritated bone under it. Nothing is torn.

The bench now has Cycle and Cycle, low saddle, and travels to 120° of bend, because cycling works the knee deeper than running does. The model is also slightly refined: near a straight knee the kneecap is now still pressed lightly into its groove, as it is in reality, which raises the walking and straight-leg numbers a little. Running is unchanged.

New in this version: the real anatomy under every figure. Each figure now has two anatomical views of your left knee that move with that figure's knee angle. Side view (from the outer side, front of the knee to the right): femur, kneecap, quadriceps and patellar tendons, tibia, fibula, meniscus and the outer collateral ligament (LCL), with the cruciate ligaments (ACL, PCL) drawn faintly because they sit inside the joint. The small Baker's cyst sits behind the knee. From below (the "sunrise" view radiologists use): the kneecap sitting in its groove, sliding outward by the model's shift, held on the inner side by the MPFL and on the outer side by the retinaculum. Blue is cartilage. Red shows load: on the tendons it scales with tendon force, and on the kneecap's cartilage with stress on the outer facet, where the small crack (the red tick) is. Drawings are schematic, not traced from your scan.

Inside one running stride

Here's a running stride on a treadmill, with your left knee's anatomy underneath following each moment. Use the slider to stop on any stage. The ones to look at are loading (just after the foot lands), where the tendons and the outer facet turn red, and swing, where the knee folds deep but carries almost nothing. Switch to Walking to see the opposite: little load, but the kneecap riding furthest outward in the shallow groove.

Why cycling hurt after a while

Per pedal stroke, cycling is easy on the kneecap. With a well-set saddle the hardest push happens at about 90° of bend, where the kneecap sits deep in its groove and presses on its largest contact patch. The model puts the outer-facet peak near 3.3 MPa, against about 11 MPa per running stride. The kneecap also hardly shifts outward, because it never gets near the shallow end of the groove.

So why did it start to hurt after some distance? Three things add up:

  • The count. At 85 rpm each knee does about 5,100 strokes an hour. Each one is gentle, but an irritable facet and two irritated tendons respond to the total, and that pain typically arrives late in a ride or after it.
  • The set-up. A saddle a few cm too low, or too far forward, plus a big gear or a climb at low cadence, means deeper bends and more torque per stroke. Toggle it in Fig 2: the peak rises to about 5.3 MPa, 60% more on every stroke. This is the classic cause of pain at the front of the knee in cyclists.
  • Knee drift. As the hip muscles tire, the knee starts to track inward at the top of the stroke. Cleats rotated wrongly, or too little float, force the same thing. On the bench that is the anchor slide moving outward: more outward pull on the kneecap.
Bike check. At the bottom of the stroke, with your heel level, the knee should stay 25–35° bent, never straight and never well bent. Keep cadence at 85–95 rpm and change down early on climbs. Your cleats should let the heel sit naturally (a little float helps), and your knee should travel straight up and down over the pedal, not inward. Done like that, cycling is one of the best ways to keep your fitness up while running load comes down.

The home programme (unchanged)

These are the six exercises from the first page. That your pain has dropped since you started working out is the best sign there is: it means the knee is responding to load. Keep these going right up to race week. Doses are under each figure.

Gym machines and lifts

The same model, run on the machines you asked about. One rule explains almost all of it. A machine that pushes on your shin (open chain) loads the kneecap most near a straight knee. A movement where your foot is on the floor or a plate (closed chain) loads it most when you're deeply bent. So limit leg extensions at the top of their range, and limit squats, presses and lunges at the bottom.

The cartilage crack: is it dangerous, and how does it heal?

The report says "a tiny linear focal full-thickness cartilage denuding and underlying subchondral bony edema overlying the lateral patellar facet". In plain words: in one small spot, a hairline line of the cartilage on the back of your kneecap has worn through to the bone, and the bone just under it is irritated, which shows up as bright "edema" on MRI. Around it the cartilage is mildly softened (chondrosis) in a few places.

Is it dangerous?
Not in an urgent sense. Small cartilage lesions like this are common on runners' MRIs, including in people with no pain, and many stay the same size for years. The real risk is slow enlargement if the same spot keeps getting overloaded. With a kneecap that rides outward, that spot is exactly where the load goes. So the goal is to calm that spot down and spread its load, not to fix the line itself.
Will it heal?
Honestly: the cartilage itself won't regrow to normal. Adult joint cartilage has no blood supply, so a full-thickness line doesn't knit back like bone or tendon. It may partly fill with tougher scar cartilage, or simply stay as it is. What does heal is the irritated bone underneath, and that's usually the main source of pain. It settles over weeks to a few months once its load is under its tolerance. Your falling pain fits that.
So what does "cured" look like?
A quiet knee. The line still shows on a scan, but it doesn't hurt, doesn't swell, and doesn't grow. You get there by lowering peak stress on the outer facet: stronger quads and hips, better tracking, a quicker running cadence, and no sudden jumps in load. Gentle, repeated loading also helps the cartilage, because it gets its nutrients from being squeezed and released. That's why cycling with a correct saddle and the exercises here are good for it, while long rest isn't.
Do I need more than exercise?
Usually not, for a lesion this small. Injections such as PRP or hyaluronic acid have mixed evidence and aren't first-line. Surgery (cartilage repair, or moving the tendon attachment to fix the tracking) is for larger lesions, repeated dislocations, or a TT-TG well above 20 mm, after months of rehab have failed. None of those describe your report. Supplements (collagen, glucosamine) are low-risk but have weak evidence.
Warning signs
The knee swells after runs (puffy, tight, hard to fully bend). It truly locks or catches and won't straighten. Pain is worse each week rather than better, or wakes you at night. Any of these means the lesion is unhappy: see your orthopaedic doctor, who may repeat the MRI.

The December marathon

You have about six weeks. Your pain is falling while you train, which is the most important fact here. Running the marathon is reasonable if three things are true: you can already run about 20 km or more without pain going above 3/10, the knee doesn't swell afterwards, and it's no worse the next morning. If one of those fails, the honest options are run-walking the whole race at an easier pace, dropping to the half, or deferring. Six weeks is too short to build both mileage and kneecap tolerance from scratch.

What the model says matters most for race day is the per-landing peak, so the cheapest wins are a quicker cadence, a run-walk rhythm from the start (walk breaks give the facet and tendon a pause before fatigue sets in and the knee starts to drift inward), and flat, even pacing, because downhills combine a deep bend with braking.

Cadence, 4:15 marathonLandings per legPeak outer-facet stress each landing
Your usual (165 spm)21,03810.8 MPa

A quicker step means slightly more landings, each one lighter. Joint stress per landing matters more than the count, which is why cadence is the cheapest change you can make. Rehab strength (Fig 1, "After rehab") stacks on top of this.

WeekFocusWhat to do
Oct 26 – Nov 1Consolidate3–4 easy runs. Long run = your longest recent pain-free run, no longer. Start the +5% cadence on every run. Strength 2× (Figs 3–12 in the green/amber rows). Bike instead of a 4th run if the knee is grumbling.
Nov 2 – 8BuildLong run +15–20 min if last week's long run followed the pain rule. Try run-walk on it (e.g. 9 min run / 1 min walk) and see how the knee feels the next morning. Strength 2×.

Nov 23 – 29TaperVolume down ~30%. Long run 16–20 km. Strength 1×, lighter: no new exercises.
Nov 30 – Dec 6Race week2–3 short easy runs with strides at race cadence. Clamshells and bridges only, early in the week. Race on the weekend.
Pain rule, every session: up to 3/10 during, settled within 24 hours, not worse the next morning. If you break it, repeat the previous week rather than pushing on. If you break it twice in a row, or see any warning sign above, stop building and see a physio or your doctor.
This page is an educational model built from your MRI report. It is not a diagnosis or a training prescription, and the numbers are estimates for a typical 75 kg person, not measurements of your knee. A sports physiotherapist who examines you, ideally with a gait and bike-fit check, should confirm the plan, and should certainly confirm it before race week.

Model sources (approximate): kneecap contact areas from Huberti & Hayes (1984); joint force from a pulley model of the quadriceps and patellar tendon with a small straight-knee offset; gait curves from standard walking and running data; cycling knee moments after Ericson (1986); open- versus closed-chain kneecap stress pattern after Steinkamp (1993) and Escamilla (1998); cadence effect from Lenhart (2014). Machine loads assume a moderate 10–12-rep-max weight.
